notes.meaning: God promises a coming ruler who will govern with fairness, truth, and honesty. Under him, leaders will uphold what is right and protect good people from harm. While godly King Hezekiah gave an early taste of this, the promise finds its true and complete home in Jesus Christ.

differ.view: The king is Jesus Christ alone rather than Hezekiah, since no earthly king can fully match what is promised here.
The prophecy pointed first to King Hezekiah as an earthly model, but points ultimately to Christ as the one who truly restores the church.
The prophecy refers directly to Hezekiah, who served as an earthly picture of Christ.

notes.meaning: Good rulers protect people from violence and provide relief to those who are hurting. In a dry and scorching desert, a massive rock provides cool shade, and running streams give life to weary travelers. In the same way, Christ protects believers from the storms of life and refreshes their souls.

When God renews His people, He cures their spiritual blindness and deafness. People who were once hasty and foolish will slow down to gain true understanding, and those who hesitated to speak of God will speak clearly and boldly. This spiritual healing began in Hezekiah's day but was accomplished fully through Christ's gospel.

Society often praises rich and selfish people as if they were generous heroes. Under a righteous reign, these false masks are stripped away and people are judged by their true character. A person who hoards wealth for himself will no longer be called honorable.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers take the word translated 'fool' or 'liberal' to refer to modern theological liberals.

notes.meaning: Foolish and ungodly people show who they are by scheming against the Lord and neglecting the poor. Crafty scoundrels even twist the legal system with lies to defeat needy people who have a just case. God exposes these wicked plots and shows that high titles cannot hide cruel deeds.

Truly generous people make wise and deliberate plans to do good to others. Their kindness is not just a quick impulse, but a steady habit guided by God. Because their lives are rooted in doing what is right, God establishes and protects them.

Isaiah calls out the wealthy women of Jerusalem who were resting in careless luxury while ignoring God. He tells them to stand up and pay attention to God's message with serious reverence. Their false sense of security was about to be shattered by coming judgment.

The ease of these confident women would not last long, for disaster would strike in just over a year. The invading armies would destroy the vineyards and orchards, leaving no grapes or fruit to harvest. Without food and wine, their careless partying would suddenly turn to hunger and fear.

The prophet urges these comfortable women to take off their fine clothes and put on sackcloth, a rough cloth worn to show deep grief and repentance. Instead of waiting for war to strip them of their wealth, they should humble themselves before God right away. Turning to God in sorrow is the only way to prepare for difficult days.

The people would beat their chests in deep sorrow over ruined fields and vineyards that once fed them. Weeds and thorns would choke the land, and even grand palaces and bustling city streets would sit empty and abandoned. Strong towers would become quiet ruins where wild donkeys roam and sheep graze, showing how sin ruins earthly pride.

Desolation will not last forever, but only until God pours out His Holy Spirit from heaven in rich abundance. When the Spirit comes, barren hearts and lands will turn into fruitful orchards, and fruitful places will flourish like thick forests. Real renewal and lasting fruitfulness can only come from God's gracious power, not human effort.

differ.view: This was fulfilled partly when the Jews returned from Babylon, and far more richly at Pentecost when the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles.
This cannot refer to Pentecost, but points forward to a future day when the Spirit brings in the fullness of the Gentiles and the conversion of the Jews.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Hebrew text literally describes new life or breath being poured out or laid bare upon the people.

notes.meaning: When the Spirit works, fairness and godly living take root everywhere, from neglected wastelands to rich fields. Doing what is right produces true peace, deep quietness, and lasting confidence. Holiness is the only real path to lasting happiness and security with God.

God promises that His people will live in safe homes and rest without fear. While worldly peace is fragile and easily broken, the peace God provides guards the heart and home. Those who trust in the Lord find true rest under His faithful care.

Before complete peace arrives, God's severe judgments will fall like crushing hail on the enemies of His people. The proud forest will be knocked down and the haughty city brought down to the ground. God humbles every worldly power that opposes Him so His people may dwell safely.

differ.view: The low-lying city represents God's people living safely in humble valleys while storms crush the proud forests of their enemies.
The forest and the fallen city represent the overthrow of Antichrist and the spiritual city of Rome in the last days.

notes.meaning: Those who live through God's judgment will enjoy rich blessings and abundant harvests. The ground will be so well-watered that crops will grow thickly, and farmers will let their oxen and donkeys graze freely without worry. This picture of joyful farming also points to the gospel, where believers scatter God's word far and wide and see rich fruit.

differ.view: The verse is a direct promise to gospel ministers in the latter days who faithfully preach the word to all kinds of people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some suggest the peaceful farming scene reflects the prophet's love of simple country life, contrasting with the empty glamour of military power.
